canonical_policy.name: No CQRS/mediator/VSA by default
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Do not introduce CQRS handlers, MediatR, Kommand, Vertical Slice Architecture or similar mediator-based organization unless explicitly approved.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Pattern approval includes service-size nonjustification; executable MediatR/Kommand prefix approval rather than semantic dispatch is explicitly registered. Post-manifest warning/removal advice is not an observed blocking package install.

Do not introduce CQRS command/query handlers, mediator libraries or mediator-based request dispatch, Vertical Slice Architecture, or similar mediator-based organization unless explicitly approved. A service growing too large is a signal to reconsider its responsibilities, not a reason to adopt another pattern.

Check against decision control (`CLAUDE.md`), the patterns not adopted (imported adopted-architecture rule), and engineering discipline before scaffolding any of: MediatR-style mediators, CQRS handler trees, Vertical Slice Architecture, Domain Events, Specifications, SharedKernel, BuildingBlocks, EventBus, messaging, microservices, Kubernetes, cloud-specific projects, state-management frameworks, Docker without a containerization need, and generic `Common`/`Helpers`/`Utils` directories.

- **Delegated** — local, reversible, and does not materially change a boundary, dependency, accepted convention, public contract, or observable behavior: decide and proceed.
- **Reserved** — requires approval: changing an accepted project/architecture decision; adopting a new architectural style or pattern (Rich Domain Model or DDD tactical patterns, CQRS, mediator-based organization, Vertical Slice Architecture, event sourcing, a project-wide Result model, microservices); adding a production project/layer or changing the project reference graph; changing persistence boundaries (for example several persistence contexts) or persistence technology; adding an infrastructure category (messaging, background processing, distributed cache, search, external storage, external identity); adding a major library/framework or replacing approved baseline technology; introducing a project-wide convention or abstraction; changing authentication/authorization architecture; a breaking public API change or adopting API versioning; defining product behavior or tunable values not defined by product sources; changing a capability selection (also requires an ADR).
- Unclear case: any "yes" makes it Reserved — does it add, remove, or replace a dependency, framework, or infrastructure capability? change a project/layer/reference boundary? establish a convention other code must follow? change observable behavior or a public contract? become expensive to reverse once other code depends on it?

canonical_policy.name: Controllers are thin HTTP entry points
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: ASP.NET Core Controllers are the default HTTP entry point; they bind/validate input, invoke Application services, and translate outcomes to HTTP responses.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Default controllers additionally mandate Controllers folder and explicit request for Minimal API groups. Version-group and validation-filter anti-patterns in Controller projects are separately registered; no generic entry-point paraphrase used to hide them.

context_quotes:
- Entry-point adapters in Api are the default HTTP entry point and stay thin: they bind and validate HTTP input, invoke Application Services, and translate outcomes into HTTP responses.
- Entry-point adapters must not contain business logic, access the persistence context or concrete repositories, or construct infrastructure services manually.

- Entry-point mechanism: ASP.NET Core Controllers (decided stack), as controller classes in a `Controllers/` folder of the entry-point project; do not create Minimal API endpoint groups unless explicitly requested.
- Transport result types that stay at the entry point: `IActionResult`, `ActionResult<T>`, `IResult`, and status-code constants.

- Decided: .NET 10 LTS (latest stable servicing release), C# 14, ASP.NET Core, ASP.NET Core Controllers. Moving to a preview/RC .NET or C# release requires approval.
- Decided: FluentValidation is the standard explicit request/use-case validation library; application logging uses `ILogger<T>` with Serilog as the provider.

Versioning without a compatibility requirement; Minimal API version-group examples in a Controller project; domain models duplicated per version; incompatible edits to an existing version; a new version for every implementation change; silently removing deprecated versions; mixing URL, header, and query versioning without a concrete reason.

Raw exception messages to clients; inconsistent anonymous error objects; use-case code depending on HTTP status codes; `Result<T>` everywhere; exceptions for every negative branch; swallowed exceptions; catch/log/rethrow at every layer; duplicate logging; sensitive data in `ProblemDetails`; business rules only in request validators; Minimal API endpoint filters for validation in a Controller project.

canonical_policy.name: Prefer specific repositories
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Prefer specific repository interfaces representing actual cohesive Application persistence needs rather than table-mirroring generic CRUD contracts.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Specific cohesive persistence needs and concrete-repository use-case queries are baseline actions; illustrative table repeats their defaults without converting all data access into fixed CRUD.

context_quotes:
- Default: prefer specific repository interfaces that represent cohesive Application persistence needs rather than generic CRUD contracts mirroring tables. Interfaces live in Application, implementations in Infrastructure.
- Application must not depend on `IGenericRepository<T>` or another generic CRUD contract; a generic repository base class may exist only inside Infrastructure, only to remove real duplication, and never as a replacement for the ORM's query capabilities.
Use-case-specific queries stay in concrete repositories, which may use the full EF Core API.

| Scenario | Default |
| --- | --- |
| Use-case persistence dependency | specific repository interface |
| Commit | `IUnitOfWork.SaveChangesAsync` |
| Read-only entity query | `AsNoTracking()` when useful |
| Read model | database-side projection |
| Primary-key entity lookup | `FindAsync` when its semantics fit |
| Complex graph | explicit `Include` or projection |
| Set-based update/delete | `ExecuteUpdateAsync` / `ExecuteDeleteAsync` when appropriate |
| Measured extremely hot query | consider a compiled query |
| Several commits that must be atomic | explicit transaction |
| Production schema change | reviewed migration, controlled deployment |
| Empty Development database | run the seeder |
| Fresh local seed data | explicitly recreate the local database |
| Test data | dedicated test setup, never the seeder |

canonical_policy.name: Unit of Work is commit boundary
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Use IUnitOfWork as the normal commit boundary for an Application use case; repositories stage changes and Application Services decide when to commit.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Named commit delegation/shared tracking, no tracked-entity caching across commit boundaries, and caution mixing bulk changes with tracked same rows are separate union constraints.

- Persistence context: the scoped `AppDbContext`, shared by every repository taking part in one use case. Persistence-implementation types: `DbContext`, `DbSet<T>`, EF Core APIs, EF-backed `IQueryable<T>`, SQL Server provider types.
- Commit boundary: the commit-boundary implementation delegates to `AppDbContext.SaveChangesAsync`; staged changes are the tracked changes of the shared context.
- Relational fidelity: the actual provider is SQL Server. EF Core InMemory, SQLite, or another provider does not establish SQL Server behavior.

Caching by default; global keys for tenant/user data; mutable data cached indefinitely; cache technology in the domain model; use-case code depending on `HybridCache` without a deliberate decision; caching tracked ORM entities across commit boundaries; cache as authoritative persistence; Redis merely because caching exists.
`DbContext` already tracks changes; `IUnitOfWork` is the use-case-facing abstraction over the same scoped context. An internal generic base may share helpers:

- **Bulk operations** — `ExecuteUpdateAsync`/`ExecuteDeleteAsync` run directly against the database and bypass change tracking; do not mix them casually with tracked entities for the same rows; understand their transaction semantics.

EF transaction APIs do not solve distributed transactions.
